title: ABG case 01
حالة غازات دم 01
vignette: A patient with a severe asthma exacerbation, working hard to breathe, now tiring.

question.prompt: Based on this gas panel, what is the acid-base interpretation?
question.explanation: PaCO2 is markedly elevated (60) causing acidemia, with HCO3- still within the normal range - there has not been time for renal compensation yet. This is uncompensated respiratory acidosis, consistent with acute ventilatory failure from severe asthma.

oxygenationNote: PaO2 65 mmHg on FiO2 0.4 gives a P/F ratio of 162.5.
evidenceSources: ERC/ESICM arterial blood gas teaching framework

title: ABG case 02
حالة غازات دم 02
vignette: A patient with new-onset diabetic ketoacidosis.

question.prompt: Based on this gas panel, what is the acid-base interpretation?
question.explanation: HCO3- is markedly low (9) causing acidemia, and PaCO2 has fallen to 22 - lower than normal but not as low as Winter's formula predicts (19.5-23.5 is actually within range here), so this is appropriate but still partial respiratory compensation for a severe metabolic acidosis, as expected in DKA.

evidenceSources: ERC/ESICM arterial blood gas teaching framework

title: ABG case 03
حالة غازات دم 03
vignette: An anxious patient hyperventilating after a panic episode.

question.prompt: Based on this gas panel, what is the acid-base interpretation?
question.explanation: PaCO2 is low (28) causing alkalemia, with HCO3- still essentially normal - the kidneys have not yet had time to compensate. This is acute, uncompensated respiratory alkalosis from hyperventilation.

evidenceSources: ERC/ESICM arterial blood gas teaching framework

title: ABG case 04
حالة غازات دم 04
vignette: A patient with prolonged vomiting and nasogastric suction losses.

question.prompt: Based on this gas panel, what is the acid-base interpretation?
question.explanation: HCO3- is elevated (34) causing alkalemia, and PaCO2 has risen to 46 - a appropriate but incomplete respiratory compensation (expected range 42.3-45.3 would be fully compensated). This is partially-compensated metabolic alkalosis, consistent with chloride and acid loss from vomiting.

evidenceSources: ERC/ESICM arterial blood gas teaching framework

title: ABG case 05
حالة غازات دم 05
vignette: A patient with longstanding COPD, at their usual baseline, feeling well.

question.prompt: Based on this gas panel, what is the acid-base interpretation?
question.explanation: pH is within normal limits despite a very high PaCO2 (80) and very high HCO3- (36). The respiratory derangement is proportionally larger than the metabolic one, and the degree of HCO3- rise fits a sustained, chronic renal response - this is fully-compensated (chronic) respiratory acidosis, the classic pattern in stable COPD.

oxygenationNote: PaO2 58 mmHg on FiO2 0.28 gives a P/F ratio of 207.1.
evidenceSources: ERC/ESICM arterial blood gas teaching framework

title: ABG case 06
حالة غازات دم 06
vignette: A patient in septic shock with lactic acidosis, now also showing early respiratory fatigue.

question.prompt: Based on this gas panel, what is the acid-base interpretation?
question.explanation: Both PaCO2 (48, should be low to compensate) and HCO3- (12, should be higher) are abnormal in the direction that worsens acidemia at the same time - the lungs cannot mount the expected compensation because they are also failing. This is a mixed respiratory and metabolic acidosis, a high-risk combination requiring urgent escalation.

oxygenationNote: PaO2 70 mmHg on FiO2 0.5 gives a P/F ratio of 140.
evidenceSources: ERC/ESICM arterial blood gas teaching framework

title: ABG case 07
حالة غازات دم 07
vignette: A ventilated patient with ARDS on a high FiO2.

question.prompt: Based on this gas panel, what is the acid-base interpretation?
question.explanation: pH, PaCO2 and HCO3- are all within normal limits - there is no acid-base disorder here. The PaO2 of 68 looks only mildly low on its own, but achieving even that required an FiO2 of 0.8 - the P/F ratio of 85 reveals severe oxygenation impairment that the raw PaO2 alone would hide.

oxygenationNote: PaO2 68 mmHg on FiO2 0.8 gives a P/F ratio of 85.
evidenceSources: ERC/ESICM arterial blood gas teaching framework
